title: How Dividends Work for Investors on the Nigerian Stock Exchange
summary: What dividends are, the qualification and payment dates that matter, how e-dividend payment works, the tax, and how to avoid unclaimed dividends.
body_markdown:
**n short:** A dividend is a share of a company’s profit paid to shareholders, usually once a year, as cash or bonus shares. To receive one, you must own the shares before the qualification date, which is not the same as the payment date. Cash dividends are paid electronically into your bank account, minus a 10% withholding tax, once your e-dividend mandate is set up. This is general information, not advice.


For many Nigerian investors, dividends are the whole point. The idea of owning a piece of a solid company and receiving a share of its profits every year, without lifting a finger, is one of the most appealing things about the stock market. Nigeria’s market has a genuinely strong dividend culture, particularly among the banks and large established companies.


But dividends come with a set of dates, rules, and one very common pitfall that catches thousands of investors every year. This guide explains what dividends are, how and when you get paid, the tax involved, and how to make sure the money that is owed to you actually reaches you. It is general information, not investment advice. If you are newer to the market, our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) covers the basics.


## What is a dividend?


A dividend is a portion of a company’s profit paid out to its shareholders, usually once a year, though some companies pay an interim dividend during the year as well. When you own shares in a company that declares a dividend, you receive an amount based on how many shares you hold.


Dividends come in two forms. A cash dividend is money paid to you, credited to your bank account. A bonus issue, sometimes called scrip, is extra shares given to you for free instead of cash, which increases the number of shares you own. Most of what people mean by “dividends” is the cash kind.


A company’s board proposes the dividend, and shareholders approve it at the Annual General Meeting (AGM). It is not automatic or guaranteed. A company can raise, cut, or skip its dividend depending on how it performs and what its directors decide, which is why a long, consistent dividend record tells you more than a single generous payout.


## The dates that matter


To receive a dividend, you must own the shares before the qualification date, and this is where most people get caught out. Several dates sit around a dividend, and confusing them is the single most common dividend mistake Nigerian investors make.


Here is what each one means. The **declaration date** is when the company announces the dividend and its amount. The **qualification date** (also called the record date) is the cut-off: you must be a registered shareholder on or before this date to receive the dividend. The **closure of register** is a short period, usually just after the qualification date, when the register is locked and no share transfers are processed. The **payment date** is when the money is actually paid out, often weeks after the qualification date.


The trap is assuming the qualification date and the payment date are the same, or that buying the shares any time before payment gets you the dividend. It does not. If you buy after the qualification date, you will not receive that dividend no matter how long you then hold the shares. And because trades take time to settle, with the NGX now settling on a T+1 basis, you should buy at least a trading day ahead of the qualification date to be sure you are on the register in time.


One more thing to expect: after the qualification date, a stock’s price often falls by roughly the dividend amount, because new buyers are no longer entitled to that payout. This is normal and is why chasing a dividend purely for the payout, without regard to the price, does not create free money.


## How dividends are paid: the e-dividend system


Cash dividends in Nigeria are paid electronically, directly into your bank account, through what is called the e-dividend system. To receive them, you need to have completed an e-dividend mandate, which links your bank account and CSCS details to the registrar that handles a company’s payouts.


This matters enormously, and it is the root of the pitfall covered in the next section. In the past, dividends were paid by posting a physical cheque, called a dividend warrant, to your registered address. That system produced huge numbers of uncashed and lost warrants, so the Securities and Exchange Commission pushed the market to electronic payments. Today, if your e-dividend mandate is properly set up, your dividends simply appear in your bank account. If it is not, the money has nowhere to go.


Setting up your mandate is done through the registrar, and a good broker helps you get this right at onboarding. If you invest through[Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , your CSCS account is set up as part of the process, which is the foundation the dividend infrastructure rests on.


## Dividend yield and what it tells you


The most common way to measure a dividend is the dividend yield, which is the annual dividend divided by the share price, shown as a percentage. If a share costs ₦100 and pays a ₦10 dividend, the yield is 10%. It tells you how much income you earn relative to the price you pay.


A higher yield looks attractive, but a yield that seems unusually high deserves caution rather than excitement. It can happen because the share price has fallen sharply, which may signal trouble, or because the payout is larger than the company can sustainably afford. A useful companion measure is the payout ratio, which is the share of profits paid out as dividends. A company paying out almost everything it earns has little room to maintain the dividend if profits dip.


So look past the headline yield to whether the dividend is sustainable and backed by a consistent record. Our[guide to choosing NGX stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-choose-nigerian-stocks-a-beginners-guide/) goes deeper on assessing a company, including its dividend track record.


## Tax on dividends


Dividends in Nigeria are subject to a withholding tax of 10%, deducted at source before the money reaches you, and reduced to 7.5% for investors covered by a tax treaty. For most individual investors, this is treated as a final tax, meaning there is nothing further to pay on that dividend and, if dividends are your only Nigerian income, generally nothing further to file.


Bonus shares are treated differently: because no cash changes hands, a bonus issue does not attract this withholding tax. For the full picture on how investment income is taxed, including the 2026 changes to capital gains, see our[guide to tax on Nigerian stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/tax-on-nigerian-stocks-what-ngx-investors-need-to-know/) .


## The unclaimed dividends problem


Nigeria has a very large unclaimed dividends problem, and there is a real chance some of that money belongs to you. Unclaimed dividends, money that companies have declared and set aside but that never reached the shareholder, are estimated at around ₦270 billion. In July 2026, the SEC[launched a nationwide campaign](https://nairametrics.com/2026/07/16/sec-launches-nationwide-campaign-to-recover-n270-billion-unclaimed-dividends/) to help investors recover these funds, driven through the National Investor Protection Fund.


The causes are almost always administrative rather than dramatic: no e-dividend mandate on file, outdated bank or contact details, warrants that were posted and never cashed, or shares inherited from a relative whose records were never updated. Two waves of retail investing, the 2004 to 2008 boom and the 2024 bank and telecoms offers, left many investors with holdings they never fully registered.


The good news is that unclaimed dividends are generally recoverable. You contact the relevant registrar with your CHN, CSCS number, and valid identification to start the process, and the SEC has reaffirmed that shareholders remain entitled to claim eligible unpaid dividends even those older than twelve years. If you think you may be owed dividends, our practical guide on[why you may not have received your NGX dividend](https://learn.investbamboo.com/why-you-havent-received-your-ngx-dividend-and-how-to-fix-it/) walks through how to fix it. The single best preventive step is to make sure your e-dividend mandate is set up correctly from the start.


## Dividends versus bonus shares


It is worth being clear on the difference, because both are called “dividends” loosely. A cash dividend puts money in your account and is subject to the 10% withholding tax. A bonus issue gives you additional shares rather than cash, increases the total number of shares you hold, and does not attract withholding tax because no money is paid out. A company may do one, the other, or both in the same year.


## Should you invest for dividends?


Dividends are a genuine source of return, and for investors who want income rather than only price growth, a company’s dividend record is an important consideration. Nigeria’s dividend culture, particularly among the banks and large consumer and industrial companies, is one reason many local investors hold shares for the long term.


That said, dividends should be one part of the picture, not the whole of it. They are never guaranteed and can be cut when a company’s fortunes change, a very high yield can be a warning rather than a bargain, and total return, the combination of dividends and price change, is what ultimately matters. Whether a dividend-focused approach suits you depends on your goals and circumstances, which is why this is general information rather than a recommendation. You can invest in[Nigerian stocks](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , including the companies known for paying dividends, on Bamboo.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is a dividend?** A dividend is a portion of a company’s profit paid to its shareholders, usually once a year, either as cash credited to your bank account or as bonus shares. The amount you receive depends on how many shares you own.


**How do I qualify to receive a dividend?** You must be a registered shareholder on or before the qualification date. Because trades take time to settle, buy the shares at least a trading day before that date. Buying after the qualification date means you will not receive that particular dividend.


**How are dividends paid in Nigeria?** Cash dividends are paid electronically into your bank account through the e-dividend system, provided you have completed an e-dividend mandate with the registrar. Physical dividend warrants have largely been discontinued.


**How much tax do I pay on dividends?** A 10% withholding tax is deducted at source, reduced to 7.5% for treaty-country investors, and it is treated as a final tax for most individuals, so there is usually nothing more to pay. Bonus shares do not attract this tax.


**How do I claim unclaimed dividends?** Contact the company’s registrar with your CHN, CSCS number, and valid ID to start the recovery process. Nigeria has around ₦270 billion in unclaimed dividends, and shareholders remain entitled to claim eligible amounts, so it is worth checking if any is yours.
